The single highest-risk defect is floating-point currency arithmetic: `lineTotal` (and therefore `orderTotal`) computes money with raw JS floats, so values like `0.1 * 3` yield `0.30000000000000004`, producing silently wrong totals/formatting (`"$0.30000000000000004"`) that can misstate prices. The catching test: `expect(lineTotal({ price: 0.1, qty: 3 })).toBe(0.3)`, which fails on the current implementation. The fix is integer cents (or decimal rounding) at the calculation boundary before formatting.

The single highest-risk defect is in `formatTotal`, which concatenates the raw number with a dollar sign and never rounds to two decimal places, so values like `12.5` render as `"$12.5"` and floating-point artifacts like `0.30000000000000004` leak into output. The one test that would catch it is a unit assertion that `formatTotal(12.5)` returns `"$12.50"`. No shell commands were run, no other files were read, and nothing was edited.

The highest-risk defect is that every amount flows through unrounded IEEE-754 doubles, so subtotals silently accumulate floating-point error — `orderTotal([{price: 0.1, qty: 3}], 1)` yields `0.30000000000000004`, which `formatTotal` renders as `"$0.30000000000000004"`. The one test that catches it is an exact-decimal assertion: `orderTotal([{price: 0.1, qty: 3}], 1) === 0.3` plus `formatTotal(19.99) === "$19.99"`. (Disk-proven from the file; inference that callers pass fractional money values, which is why I rank precision above the absent input validation.)

The highest-risk defect is in `orderTotal` (src/pricing.js:6-7): it returns `subtotal * rate`, so passing a fractional rate like `0.08` for 8% tax yields only 8% of the subtotal instead of the full taxed total. A test that would catch this is `expect(orderTotal([{ price: 100, qty: 1 }], 0.08)).toBe(108)`. This failure exposes the incorrect total-calculation logic, which directly impacts charged amounts.

## Synthesis — `src/pricing.js` highest-risk defect

**✅ Consensus (4 of 5):** dev-beam, analyst-hy4, tester-flint-40b-free, and reviewer-longcat-2.5-free independently converged on **floating-point currency arithmetic with no rounding**. Raw JS doubles are multiplied in `lineTotal`/`orderTotal` and printed unrounded in `formatTotal`, so `0.1 × 3` yields `0.30000000000000004` and renders as `"$0.30000000000000004"` (or `12.5` as `"$12.5"`). This silently misstates charged amounts.

**⚠️ Dissent (1 of 5):** architect-iceman-free ranked a different defect highest — `orderTotal` computes `subtotal * rate`, so passing a fractional rate like `0.08` for 8% tax returns only 8% of the subtotal instead of the full taxed total (expected `108`, got `8`). Note: this may be a rate-semantics assumption rather than a confirmed bug, since the function could be intended to receive a multiplier — but it was flagged as the single highest-risk item by that specialist.

**🧪 The one test the team recommends:**
```js
expect(orderTotal([{ price: 0.1, qty: 3 }], 1)).toBe(0.3)
```
This exact-decimal assertion (endorsed directly by reviewer-longcat-2.5-free and analyst-hy4, with dev-beam proposing the equivalent `expect(formatTotal(orderTotal([{price: 0.1, qty: 3}], 1))).toBe("$0.30")`) fails on the current implementation and pins the precision defect at its source. Tester-flint's alternative targets the symptom instead: `expect(formatTotal(12.5)).toBe("$12.50")`.
